title: Insulating a conservatory polycarbonate roof
subtitle: Comparing cellular board, foil lining, and replacement options for a cold conservatory roof
excerpt: A standard 6 mm polycarbonate conservatory roof has a U-value around 3.8 W/m²K, roughly four times worse than a modern double-glazed window. This guide covers the three main approaches to improving it: a foil-lined cellular infill panel, a solid insulated replacement board, and a full roof conversion.
sourceNotes: LABC (Local Authority Building Control) guidance on conservatory roof replacements and Part L notification thresholds. Energy Saving Trust technical briefings on conservatory thermal performance. BRE Information Paper IP 14/10 on solid and polycarbonate conservatory roofs.

glossaryTerms.definition: A measure of how quickly heat passes through a building element. Lower is better. Units are W/m²K.
A path through a building element that conducts heat more readily than the surrounding material, creating a cold spot.
A membrane that limits the movement of water vapour through a building element, reducing condensation risk.

content.text: A standard twin-wall polycarbonate conservatory roof loses heat at a rate of around 3.8 W/m²K. For a 15 m² roof, that is roughly 450 W of heat loss for every degree of temperature difference between inside and outside. On a cold day in January, that is 2,000 to 3,000 W leaving through the roof alone.

Three practical routes exist: installing a foil-lined cellular infill panel that slots into the existing bars, replacing the polycarbonate sheets with solid insulated boards, or replacing the entire roof structure with a solid tiled or glass roof. The first costs least and cuts the
U-value
to around 1.0 W/m²K. The second achieves a similar result with a finished look. The third achieves 0.15 to 0.18 W/m²K and may trigger Part L notification.
What you need to know first
Measure each roof panel individually. Polycarbonate sheets are rarely uniform across a conservatory; a run of eight bays may contain three different widths.

A full roof replacement is notifiable under Part L if the conservatory is over 30 m² or if the original glazed roof was part of a planning consent. Check with your Local Planning Authority before ordering.

Check the existing roof bars for signs of failure: corrosion on aluminium bars, split gaskets, or deflection. A heavy infill panel can overload a lightweight bar system. Bar-to-beam connections need inspection before adding load.

All three approaches create a warmer roof interior in winter. A warmer surface reduces the risk of condensation forming on the underside of the polycarbonate. If the existing sheets have internal misting between the twin walls, replace the sheets first rather than lining over them.
Option 1: foil-lined cellular infill panels

Foil-faced cellular panels are cut to fit between the roof bars and held in place by the existing glazing gaskets and cover strips. They are reversible and require no structural work. The foil layer reflects radiant heat back into the conservatory in winter and blocks some solar gain in summer.
Measure the clear aperture of each bay (inside face of bar to inside face of adjacent bar) in both directions. Note the depth of the glazing rebate.
Order panels cut to size, or cut 50 mm cellular polycarbonate board with a fine-toothed saw. Cut the foil facing on the reverse with a utility knife and straight edge.
Slide each panel into the glazing channel. Check it sits flat and that the existing cover strip will re-engage over the edge. Press the cover strip back using a rubber mallet and a timber offcut.
Seal any gap between the panel edge and the bar with a thin bead of neutral-cure silicone. This prevents condensation forming in the rebate.
Option 2: replacing sheets with solid insulated boards

Solid PIR-faced composite boards achieve a U-value of 0.5 to 1.0 W/m²K depending on thickness. They are heavier than polycarbonate. Verify bar-to-beam load capacity before fitting boards above 25 kg/m². A
thermal bridge
at each aluminium bar will remain; the improvement applies only to the panel area.
Option 3: full roof replacement

A solid insulated roof replaces the glazing bars and panels with a tiled or solid-glass structure. U-values of 0.15 to 0.18 W/m²K are achievable. This is the only approach that eliminates the thermal bridging at every bar. It also requires a
vapour control layer
on the warm side of the insulation. Full roof replacement is installer-only work.
Common variations
Lean-to roofs are the easiest to panel. Hip-and-valley and Edwardian shapes require more cutting.
Listed buildings: infill panels are usually fine without consent. Solid roof replacements need listed building consent.
North-facing conservatories get little winter sun. Foil-lined panels give the same warmth benefit as on a south-facing roof, with no loss of light.
What done well looks like

Panels sit flat. Cover strips are fully re-engaged. The surface on the underside of the roof no longer drops below the indoor dew point on cold nights. A thermal-imaging check will show bars as cold spots, but panel zones are noticeably warmer.
What done badly looks like

Panels cut too short and sitting on one rail only, leaving a gap at the other end. Cover strips not fully re-seated, leaving the panel edge unsupported. Foil layer installed facing down rather than up, reducing its reflective benefit.
Troubleshooter

rows.symptom: Panel bows or sags between bars after fitting
rows.cause: Panel thickness too low for the bay span, or panel was stored rolled
rows.fix: Use a minimum 25 mm thick board for spans over 500 mm. Store panels flat for 48 hours before fitting to let them relax.

rows.symptom: Condensation forms on the foil face of the panel
rows.cause: Warm moist air is reaching the cold foil surface through an unsupported gap at the panel edge
rows.fix: Seal the perimeter of each panel with low-modulus silicone before replacing the cover strip.

rows.symptom: Cover strip will not re-engage after inserting panel
rows.cause: Panel is slightly too thick for the glazing rebate
rows.fix: Reduce panel thickness by 1 to 2 mm using a fine-tooth saw or belt sander along the edge. Do not force the cover strip; a split cover strip cannot be re-used.
